title: Time-Reversal Symmetry in Artificial Topological Graphene Rings
authors: J. A. da Silva Neto, G. Q. Garcia, A. M. de M. Carvalho, C. Furtado
abstract: We study an artificial graphene ring described by the low-energy two-valley Dirac Hamiltonian with a uniform mass term. When the ring is threaded by an Aharonov-Bohm flux, the problem reduces to a second-order radial equation solved by Bessel functions. We give the exact secular equation and, for narrow rings, closed expressions for the spectrum and the persistent current. We then add a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane. The radial problem is solved with confluent hypergeometric functions, and the persistent current and magnetization are written as derivatives of a secular determinant from which the spurious roots have been removed. Besides the usual orbital coupling, the field enters through a valley-dependent term that comes from the Dirac structure and lifts the valley degeneracy. A weak-field expansion, accurate up to corrections of order B^4, gives this valley splitting explicitly and separates the diamagnetic and paramagnetic contributions to the susceptibility. Finally, we work out what time reversal implies for the spectrum. Physical time reversal, which exchanges the valleys, leads to an exact relation between levels at opposite fields. The effective single-valley time reversal, on the other hand, is broken by the mass term and by the boundary conditions, yet leaves no trace in the zero-field spectrum. Numerical results for the spectrum, the persistent current, and the magnetization illustrate the analysis.
summary: This paper theoretically analyzes the electronic properties of artificial graphene rings threaded by magnetic flux and a perpendicular magnetic field. By solving the associated radial differential equations, the authors determine the energy spectrum and persistent current. Key findings include the explicit demonstration of time-reversal symmetry relations and the calculation of magnetic response via weak-field expansions.
main_problem: The study investigates the energy spectrum and persistent current in artificial graphene rings subjected to both an Aharonov-Bohm flux and a perpendicular magnetic field.
main_result: The analysis yields an exact time-reversal symmetry relation for the energy levels and provides weak-field expansions for the valley splitting and magnetic susceptibility.
method: The authors solve the resulting radial differential equations (Bessel or confluent hypergeometric) by imposing boundary conditions on the annulus, leading to a secular determinant whose zeros define the energy eigenvalues.
model_or_system: The system is an artificial graphene ring modeled by a low-energy two-valley Dirac Hamiltonian. The physics is governed by the interplay between the Aharonov-Bohm flux and the perpendicular magnetic field, which modifies the radial equation.
key_observables: Energy spectrum ($E_{n,l,s}$), persistent current ($I$), and magnetization ($M$).
important_parameters: Aharonov-Bohm flux ($\phi$), perpendicular magnetic field ($B$), and the flux quantum ($\phi_0 = 2\pi/e$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on solving the radial equation via Bessel or confluent hypergeometric functions, and uses a weak-field expansion accurate up to $O(B^4)$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the graphene ring geometry, compare exact vs. narrow-ring energy levels vs. flux, and show the magnetization vs. flux, highlighting symmetry and level crossings.
paper_structure: The paper first analyzes the pure Aharonov-Bohm flux case using Bessel functions, then extends the analysis to include a uniform magnetic field, solving the modified radial equation using confluent hypergeometric functions. Finally, it derives the persistent current and magnetization using weak-field expansions and analyzes the implications of time-reversal symmetry.
why_interesting: The detailed treatment of topological features (Dirac Hamiltonian) coupled with external fields (flux/magnetism) and the explicit derivation of symmetry relations are highly relevant for understanding topological phases in condensed matter systems.
